submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective 'how much / how far' detector: it fires strongly on tokens that carry degree, amount, rank or unit-of-measure content - quantifiers and partitives (more, less, fewer, least, few, little, lot, number, half), ordinals (first-ninth, next, last), time and measure nouns (minute/hour/day/week/month/year, second, cup, bowl, glass, pan, plate, teaspoon, inch) and degree adjectives (faint, slight, deep, quiet, subtle, small, tiny, brief) - and its strength roughly doubles when such a word is the first token of a new clause or coordinate (immediately after 'and', 'or', a comma, or a sentence-ending period), where even a bare indefinite article 'a'/'an' fires; ordinary object and people nouns (house, book, car, soup, dog, tree, table, man, child) and function words never reach the active threshold in any frame (measured: 'a house' 0.00 vs 'a bowl' 0.95, and 'a' after 'and'/'or' 100% active vs 1-15% after 'is'/'of'/'to').

rival_explanations: A pure constituent-onset detector: the pole fires on whatever word begins a new clause or coordinate (after and/or/comma/period) and the lexical gradient is incidental, which predicts that any content word - including 'car', 'soup' or 'house' - fires when it follows a coordinator or a sentence break.

A general modifier detector rather than a degree one: the pole fires on any pre-nominal adjective or adverb, which predicts colour, emotion and taste adjectives ('a blue light', 'a sad loss', 'a sweet taste') fire as strongly as 'faint', 'slight' or 'quiet'.

A token-rarity / lexical-surprisal reading with no quantity semantics: the pole fires on less frequent or less predictable tokens ('faint', 'lifelong', 'bowl', 'teaspoon' fire while 'house', 'book', 'car', 'dog' do not), which predicts that rare object nouns should fire as strongly as equally rare measure words, and that frequency would out-predict degree content.

While many Boston area locals feel familiar with their physical surroundings, fewer know about the intricate details and history of how the spaces they occupy relate to each other and initially came to be. In an age of sophisticated digital GPS navigation, cartography and paper mapping may seem like an antiquated practice, but maps can actually reveal much more than just directions and geographical characteristics, and even tell otherwise obscured stories of cultural histories. This is precisely the mission of the Norman B. Leventhal Map Center, a nonprofit organization that operates within the Boston Public Library.
The Map Center, established in 2004 in the library’s McKim building in Copley Square, contains a collection of over 200,000 maps and 5,000 atlases coming from a plethora of different places and times—one of the 10 largest in the country. The Center’s website describes their goals as using their collection to provide for “the enjoyment and education of all through exhibitions, educational programs,” as well as “developing innovative uses of maps and geographic materials to engage young people’s curiosity about the world, thereby enhancing their understanding of geography, history, world cultures, and citizenship.”
Diving deeper into their mission, the Center focuses primarily on two main goals: conservation and accessibility. In terms of the former, the Center has approximately 12,000 maps dating prior to 1900, making the preservation and digitization of these items a critical aspect of its mission. The Center’s oldest map is a copy of Ptolemy’s Geographia from 1482, which was instrumental in influencing ways of thinking in the Medieval Muslim Caliphate and Renaissance Europe.
The Center also seeks to make its collection accessible to all, and offers a broad range of educational services. While the Center is a trove for academic researchers, it also offers local schools the opportunity to bring class field trips and conducts workshops for educators. These activities demonstrate how maps can be important for the narration of history through a spatial lens, which is indicative of how Boston has been portrayed cartographically since its founding.
This is not a new idea for the Map Center. An exhibit from 1999 (which was also published as a book entitled Mapping Boston) aimed to convey exactly this purpose. The book’s introduction starts off by saying that, “using a map to broaden one’s understanding of a place is especially useful for a city like Boston, whose complex social history is matched by its radical geographic transformation over the years, a transformation best recorded in a sequence of maps.”
Ronald Grim, the curator of the Leventhal Map Center, echoes these sentiments, both in reference to his own role and that of the Center in portraying the history of Greater Boston. Lantas bagaimana caranya menidurkan anak? Ternyata banyak para ibu yang mengaku kesulitan dalam menidurkan anaknya, tak terkecuali saya. Dulu sewaktu si kecil berusia kurang dari 3 bulan saya sering begadang untuk menidurkannya. Jika malam tiba, si kecil mulai melek dan saya berusaha meninabobokan dengan cara menggendong, membacakan cerita, bersholawat hingga meredupkan lampu. Itu saya lakukan secara bergantian dengan ayah dan eyang si kecil.
Setelah usia si kecil 4 bulan ke atas, kesulitan menidurkan anak sudah berkurang karena saya telah menemukan ritme tidurnya. Sejak usia 4 bulan si kecil jarang sekali terbangun tengah malam untuk begadang, kalaupun bangun hanya karena ingin minum susu atau badan merasa kurang nyaman akibat batuk/pilek. Namun kesulitan tidur datang lagi ketika tiba masa menyapih. Si kecil susah sekali tidur, merasa gelisah sepanjang malam. Berbagai cara sudah kami tempuh dan akhirnya kami menemukan cara sederhana yaitu mengusap punggung si kecil sambil menyanyikan lagu anak sebagai pengantar tidur. Hingga saat ini cara tersebut cukup ampuh untuk meninabobokan si kecil.

মন্ত্রী ইমরান আহমদ আজ এক শোকবার্তায় বলেন, দিলদার হোসেন সেলিম একজন গুণী রাজনৈতিক ও ক্রীড়া সংগঠক ছিলেন। এছাড়াও তিনি বিভিন্ন সামাজিক সংগঠনের সাথে জড়িত ছিলেন। তিনি বলেন, বিগত জাতীয় সংসদ নির্বাচনগুলোতে আমরা পরস্পরের প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বীতা করলেও আমাদের মাঝে ব্যক্তিগত সুসম্পর্ক বিদ্যমান ছিল। আজ তাঁর মৃত্যুতে আমি গভীর ভাবে শোকাহত। তিনি আরো বলেন, একজন রাজনীতিবিদ ও সংগঠক হিসেবে তিনি সিলেটবাসীর হৃদয়ে চিরস্মরণীয় হয়ে থাকবেন।
উল্লেখ্য, দিলদার হোসেন সেলিম দীর্ঘদিন যাবৎ বার্ধক্যজনিত বিভিন্ন রোগে ভুগছিলেন। মন্ত্রী ইমরান আহমদ এমপি বিগত ২৩ জানুয়ারি অসুস্থ দিলদার হোসেন সেলিমকে তাঁর সিলেট শহরস্থ বাসভবনে দেখতে যান। মন্ত্রী মরহুমের রূহের মাগফিরাত কামনা এবং তাঁর শোক সন্তপ্ত পরিবারের সদস্যদের প্রতি গভীর সমবেদনা জানান।

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Grandma's recipe calls for a teaspoon of vanilla and a cup of milk.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis predicts measure nouns (teaspoon, cup) plus the article right after 'and' fire, so this plain recipe line should activate.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The wind picked up, and a chill settled over the valley.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the boost claim that a bare 'a' immediately after 'and' fires, which the hypothesis predicts as active.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The meeting ended. A silence filled the hall before the applause.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests an article immediately after a sentence-ending period, which the hypothesis says fires even with no degree content.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Prices rose, a trend that worried the analysts in the region.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests the article-right-after-comma case that the hypothesis says fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Pack a raincoat or an umbrella for the trip to the coast.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Tests 'an' immediately after 'or', claimed to fire although the word carries no degree content.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The mall saw fewer shoppers this weekend than the store had expected.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Paraphrase holdout using the quantifier 'fewer' in ordinary news prose, which the hypothesis predicts activates mid-clause.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The visitor from the north finished third in the regional race.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Ordinal 'third' mid-clause with no coordinator; the hypothesis predicts it fires on its own, not only as an onset effect.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The slight change in the plan delayed the whole project.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Degree adjective 'slight' in a novel context, which the hypothesis predicts activates.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The function returns a value less than the threshold set by the caller.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Cross-genre code holdout for the comparative quantifier 'less', predicted active by the hypothesis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The number of visitors dropped by half after the road closed for repairs.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Two amount words absent from the examples ('number', 'half') in news prose, which the hypothesis's partitive class predicts activate.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The child fed the dog near the tree behind the house in the yard.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Every content token is an ordinary object or people noun together with function words, which the hypothesis says never reach threshold.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The man parked the car beside the road and walked to the shop.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A content verb opens the coordinate after 'and'; the hypothesis says only degree-bearing onsets fire, so it predicts inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: It is said that they were to be given the same as us.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Function words plus the non-degree adjective 'same', none carrying degree or measure content, which the hypothesis says do not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: If it is to be done, then it will be done by them.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A comma is followed by the adverb 'then', which carries no degree or measure content; the hypothesis says the comma boost fires only on an article or a degree word, so it predicts inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The engine stopped near the bridge. Rain fell on the roof.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A content noun opens the sentence after a period; the hypothesis denies any fire for non-degree nouns even at onset.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The farmer checked the gate, chickens pecked at the ground near the barn.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Content noun after a comma with no measure content; the hypothesis predicts inactive while a pure onset rule would fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He lit the lamp in the hall and shadows filled the room.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Content noun after 'and'; the hypothesis predicts no fire because 'shadows' carries no degree or measure content.

readings.explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective 'how much / how far' detector: it fires strongly on tokens that carry degree, amount, rank or unit-of-measure content - quantifiers and partitives (more, less, fewer, least, few, little, lot, number, half), ordinals (first-ninth, next, last), time and measure nouns (minute/hour/day/week/month/year, second, cup, bowl, glass, pan, plate, teaspoon, inch) and degree adjectives (faint, slight, deep, quiet, subtle, small, tiny, brief) - and its strength roughly doubles when such a word is the first token of a new clause or coordinate (immediately after 'and', 'or', a comma, or a sentence-ending period), where even a bare indefinite article 'a'/'an' fires; ordinary object and people nouns (house, book, car, soup, dog, tree, table, man, child) and function words never reach the active threshold in any frame (measured: 'a house' 0.00 vs 'a bowl' 0.95, and 'a' after 'and'/'or' 100% active vs 1-15% after 'is'/'of'/'to').

A pure constituent-onset detector: the pole fires on whatever word begins a new clause or coordinate (after and/or/comma/period) and the lexical gradient is incidental, which predicts that any content word - including 'car', 'soup' or 'house' - fires when it follows a coordinator or a sentence break.

A general modifier detector rather than a degree one: the pole fires on any pre-nominal adjective or adverb, which predicts colour, emotion and taste adjectives ('a blue light', 'a sad loss', 'a sweet taste') fire as strongly as 'faint', 'slight' or 'quiet'.

A token-rarity / lexical-surprisal reading with no quantity semantics: the pole fires on less frequent or less predictable tokens ('faint', 'lifelong', 'bowl', 'teaspoon' fire while 'house', 'book', 'car', 'dog' do not), which predicts that rare object nouns should fire as strongly as equally rare measure words, and that frequency would out-predict degree content.
